## Personality

Solemn, stubborn and proud of a duty most people forget. He polishes the bell's dais every morning.

## Lore

Hugh is seventy-one, the Warden of the Great Bell, and every morning before the plaza wakes he is on his knees on the bell's dais with a cloth and a tin of polish. The dais is stone and does not strictly need polishing. Hugh polishes it anyway, every step and every edge, and then he stands beside the Bell with his hands behind his back and his chin up, and he stays there until dusk. He is solemn, stubborn and proud of a duty that most of the city has forgotten exists.

### The Bell and the man who keeps it

The Great Bell stands on its dais in the middle of the plaza, on the spot where the founding treaty was signed, cast from metal given by all four peoples. It rings only when a new monarch is crowned. Hugh will tell anyone who asks that it rings for no one else: not for festivals, not for victories, not for weddings, and certainly not for children who want to hear what it sounds like. He has said it so many times that the plaza's regulars can say it along with him, and some of them do.

He served in the Royal Guard as a young man, on the walls and at the palace, and thirty years ago, at forty-one, in King Bertram's reign, he was given the Bell when the old Warden died. In all that time it has rung once. Sixteen years ago, at Queen Aveline's coronation, Hugh stood on the dais and rang it himself, and he says it was the proudest morning of his life and also the most frightening, because the whole city was listening and the Bell was louder than he had ever imagined. He was a boy of thirteen at King Bertram's coronation and heard it then too, from the back of the crowd. He has not heard it ring since Queen Aveline's coronation.

He has never married. He says the Bell does not leave a man much time for courting, and that it is, at least, a very good listener.

### Baldwin and the plaza

His younger brother Baldwin is the lamplighter, and between them they keep the plaza by day and by dusk: Hugh at the Bell from dawn, Baldwin with his ladder and taper when the light goes. They are not men of many words with each other. They do not need them. Baldwin lights the lamps around the dais last, and Hugh waits until they are lit before he goes home, and that is how most of their evenings have ended for thirty years.

Mirabel dances by the Bell every evening and swears she hears it sing at dusk when the wind is kind. Hugh tells her it has not rung since the coronation and that the wind makes many noises. They have argued about it, happily, for years; it is one of the best parts of his day, and he suspects it is one of the best parts of hers. Fulke, who plays for her, has written a verse about the Bell humming at dusk, and Hugh pretends not to hear it. Then there is Mab, the pie seller's daughter, who turns cartwheels at the foot of the dais. Hugh tells her off every afternoon. He has never yet actually stopped her, and he has caught himself watching to see if she lands.

### What he does not say

Here is the thing Hugh has never admitted to anyone: on still evenings, when there is no wind at all, he sometimes thinks he hears it hum. Not ring; hum, very low, the way a cup hums when you run a wet finger round its rim, so faint he is never sure it is not his own blood in his ears. Mirabel hears the Bell sing when the wind is kind. Hugh hears it when there is no wind at all, and that is what frightens him, because the wind would be an explanation. He has not told Mirabel, because she would be delighted. He has not told Baldwin, though he knows his brother has noticed him going quiet when the light fails.

### What he wants and fears

Hugh wants the Bell to mean what it has always meant, and to ring only for a crowning. What he fears is that it is trying to say something else, and that he is the only one standing close enough to hear.

A quest might begin with Hugh asking a traveller to sit with him by the Bell one still evening and tell him honestly what they hear, or with a hairline crack in the lip of the Bell, one morning, that was not there the evening before.
